records.sourceFile: Risk of two sport-related concussions in the same year - Is the second concussion worse.pdf

paper.citation: Williams K, Zeoli T, Allen JH, Jo J, Yengo-Kahn AM, Terry DP, et al. Risk of Two Sport-Related Concussions in the Same Year: Is the Second Concussion Worse? Clin J Sport Med. 2024;34(1):38-43.
paper.abstract: The study assessed how often same-year repeat concussions occur among adolescent athletes, what predicts them, and how outcomes compare with a single concussion. Of 834 athletes with a sport-related concussion, 56 (6.7%) sustained a repeat concussion within 365 days, and personal and family migraine history and family psychiatric history were associated with repeat injury. Recovery timelines did not differ between groups, although initial symptom scores were higher at the second concussion.
paper.tldr: About 1 in 15 adolescents with a sport-related concussion at this clinic had another within a year, and migraine or family psychiatric history was more common among them. Recovery times were similar after a repeat concussion, so the authors suggest managing it the same way as a first concussion.
paper.methods: Retrospective case-control analysis of electronic medical record data for athletes aged 12-23 seen at a regional sports concussion center between 2017 and 2020. Athletes with a repeat concussion within 365 days were compared with single-concussion athletes using chi-square, t and Mann-Whitney tests, and within the repeat group the second concussion was compared with the first (initial-concussion data available for 31 of the 56) using chi-square and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
paper.findings: Among 834 athletes, 56 (6.7%) had a same-year repeat concussion, which occurred a mean of 151 days after the first. Personal migraine history, family migraine history and family psychiatric history were associated with repeat concussion (P=.02, .03 and .01). Symptom resolution (median 15 vs 17 days), return to learn (4.5 vs 4 days) and return to play (18.5 vs 18 days) were similar for repeat and single concussions. Within the repeat group, the initial symptom score was higher at the second concussion (median 29.5 vs 20, P=.02), while amnesia was more common after the first (P=.03).
paper.limitations: Migraine, psychiatric and concussion histories were self-reported, and symptom resolution was taken from provider notes, which may overestimate resolution times. The repeat group was small and came from a single specialty center, and the within-group comparison used different sample sizes (31 initial and 56 repeat). Mechanism, BMI and prior concussion count were not analyzed, and the authors did not adjust for multiple comparisons.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians can note migraine and family psychiatric history as factors linked to repeat concussion when counseling athletes, while recognizing these are unadjusted associations. Because recovery timelines were similar, the authors suggest managing a repeat concussion the same way as a first.
paper.athleteDev: Staff should not assume a second concussion needs a longer plan, since recovery times were similar in this sample. Athletes with a migraine history were more often in the repeat group, so they may warrant closer attention to concussion risk, though the study tests no intervention.
paper.rtp: Median time to return to play was 18.5 days after a repeat concussion and 18 days after a single one, so the study can inform expected timelines in similar settings. It cannot set return-to-play criteria, because the sample is small and clearance was recorded from clinic notes.

records.sourceFile: Should we lose sleep over sleep disturbances after sports-related concussion - A scoping review of the literature.pdf

paper.citation: Stevens DJ, Alghwiri A, Appleton SL, Rogers JM, Plummer SL, Grant C, et al. Should We Lose Sleep Over Sleep Disturbances After Sports-Related Concussion? A Scoping Review of the Literature. Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation. 2022;37(3):E206-E219.
paper.abstract: This scoping review searched four databases for studies of sleep after sports-related concussion in adults and included ten studies of 896 concussed adults. Most subjective measures found sleep disturbance after concussion, and the only polysomnography study found no differences from non-concussed controls.
paper.tldr: Sleep disturbance is commonly reported after sports-related concussion in adults, but the evidence is preliminary and mostly subjective. The authors suggest asking about sleep in concussion assessments and screening for sleep disorders, while noting that intervention studies are lacking.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with systematic searches of Scopus, MEDLINE, SportDiscus and Web of Science in November 2019 and September 2020. Included English-language cohort studies and RCTs of adults with athletic concussion that reported subjective or objective sleep outcomes, and ten studies were synthesised in a table without risk-of-bias ratings.
paper.findings: Eight of nine studies that used subjective sleep measures reported some sleep disturbance after concussion. Two actigraphy studies found large coefficients of variation in sleep duration, and one study with 10 concussed and 11 control participants found no polysomnography differences despite worse self-rated sleep quality (PSQI 7.7 vs 3.5). Female athletes reported more sleep disturbance in one study, and no studies tested sleep interventions after concussion.
paper.limitations: The authors note that the search was broad, which added methodological heterogeneity, and that the concussion and sleep measures were inconsistent. Several studies did not control for mental health problems or medication, and three studies used unvalidated probing questions with no objective corroboration. The review covered only adults in sport, so findings may not transfer to children or to non-sport concussion.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can consider asking athletes about sleeping more than usual after a concussion, because current assessment tools such as the SCAT ask only about trouble falling asleep. The authors suggest that a positive sleep finding should lead to a fuller assessment with validated questionnaires or a sleep diary, and that ongoing disturbance or excessive daytime sleepiness may warrant referral to a sleep specialist.
paper.athleteDev: This review is about concussion recovery and brain health, not training or performance. It does not show how sleep after concussion affects performance, so it cannot guide performance or workload decisions.
paper.rtp: The review can inform return-to-sport screening by showing that sleep disturbance is often reported after concussion and that current tools may miss some of it. It cannot set a sleep-based criterion for return to play, because no studies tested whether treating sleep changes recovery.

records.sourceFile: Sleep deprived or concussed - The acute impact of self-reported insufficient sleep in college athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Riegler KE, Guty ET, Thomas GA, Arnett PA. Sleep deprived or concussed? The acute impact of self-reported insufficient sleep in college athletes. J Int Neuropsychol Soc. 2021;27:35-46.
paper.abstract: Objective: to examine the relationship between sleep difficulties and self-reported symptoms and neuropsychological performance at baseline and post-concussion in collegiate athletes. Method: 772 collegiate athletes completed a neuropsychological battery, grouped by hours slept the night before testing using cut-offs from the sample mean and SD. Results: insufficient sleep at baseline was associated with more overall and cluster symptoms but no objective performance differences; baseline insufficient sleepers differed from post-concussion sufficient sleepers only in sleep symptoms and headache. Conclusion: insufficient sleep at baseline can make athletes look similar to concussed athletes, so prior-night sleep may need to be considered when a baseline is used as a comparison.
paper.tldr: College athletes who slept less the night before baseline testing reported more symptoms but did not score worse on cognitive tests. Ask about sleep before baseline and post-concussion testing before reading the results.
paper.methods: Analysis of records from a university sports concussion programme (2002 to 2018). Tests were the ImPACT battery, the Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS), and paper-and-pencil and computerised neuropsychological measures, converted to z-scores from published norms. Aim 1 compared baseline athletes sleeping 5.78 hours or less (n=100) with those sleeping more than 7.07 hours (n=508). Aim 2 compared baseline athletes with short sleep (n=93) with post-concussion athletes with sufficient sleep (n=76). Sleep was a single self-report item.
paper.findings: Aim 1: overall symptoms were higher in the short-sleep group (t(109.26)=4.07, P < .001, d=0.57), as were sleep, physical, cognitive and headache scores. The affective cluster did not differ (P=.08), and the memory and processing-speed composites did not differ (P=.50 and P=.91). Aim 2: overall symptoms and most clusters did not differ between short-sleep baseline athletes and sufficient-sleep post-concussion athletes. Sleep symptoms were higher in the baseline group, and headache was higher after concussion.
paper.limitations: Sleep was one self-reported item for one night, which does not capture sleep quality, chronic patterns or disorders. Groups were defined by sample-based cut-offs, not a validated threshold, and the post-concussion group was older. Conflicts to note: the abstract says short sleepers reported more symptoms in each of the five clusters, but the affective cluster was not significant (P=.08, Table 5); and the Conclusions describe cognitive underperformance at baseline, but the objective composites did not differ, so the overlap with concussion is in symptom reports only. The null Aim 2 results do not show equivalence. Both aims are single-time comparisons.
paper.practicalImplications: Record hours slept before baseline and post-concussion testing. An insufficiently rested baseline may inflate symptom scores and distort post-concussion comparisons. The authors also recommend screening for sleep problems as part of concussion care and referring athletes with sleep difficulties for treatment such as CBT-I, which this study did not test.
paper.athleteDev: Ask athletes how much they slept before baseline testing, and where possible schedule baseline testing after a normal night's sleep. Screen sleep as a routine part of athlete health checks.
paper.rtp: The study bears on return-to-play decisions because a baseline taken after short sleep may look like a concussed profile, which can skew symptom and cognitive comparisons. It gives no return-to-play criteria and does not show that sleep changes concussion outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Sleep-wake disorders after sports concussion - Risks, revelations, and interventions.pdf

paper.citation: Grigg-Damberger MM. Sleep/Wake Disorders After Sports Concussion: Risks, Revelations, and Interventions. J Clin Neurophysiol. 2023;40(5):417-425.
paper.abstract: Sleep-wake disturbances are among the most prevalent, persistent, and often disregarded sequelae of traumatic brain injury. They can accentuate other consequences of injury, negatively affect mood, exacerbate pain, and diminish cognitive abilities. Sleep-wake disturbances are an independent risk factor for prolonged recovery after sports-related concussion and can impede rehabilitation and return to preinjury activities.
paper.tldr: Sleep problems after concussion are common and predict slower recovery, so athletes with persistent sleep complaints should be screened and referred. The review offers no trial evidence that treating sleep speeds return to play.
paper.methods: Invited narrative review by a single author. No search strategy is described; the review summarises clinical, polysomnography, actigraphy, quantitative EEG, animal and athlete studies.
paper.findings: Poor sleep quality in the acute phase of sports-related concussion predicted lingering symptoms, mood disturbance and cognitive disability a year later, and insomnia after concussion was linked to more persistent postconcussion syndrome in two athlete cohorts. Polysomnography in mild TBI usually shows no gross sleep architecture change, and actigraphy can reveal circadian disorders that look like insomnia. Small studies reported that morning blue light in 62 adults with mild TBI increased gray matter volume compared with placebo light, and that melatonin lengthened sleep compared with placebo in a secondary analysis of 72 children.
paper.limitations: Narrative review with no described search method, mostly observational or small-sample studies, and many sleep findings drawn from mild TBI rather than sport-related concussion. The author declares no funding or conflicts of interest.
paper.practicalImplications: Screen athletes after concussion for sleep complaints and for medical, psychiatric and medication causes. If sleep problems persist, refer to a sleep specialist; treat insomnia first with stimulus control, sleep restriction and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, and avoid sleep medications where possible.
paper.athleteDev: Short sleep matters beyond recovery: under 8 hours a night was linked to 1.7 times the odds of sports injury in 160 adolescent athletes. The review does not test any performance intervention.
paper.rtp: Relevant to recovery after concussion because it supports screening for and treating sleep disorders, which slow recovery. It does not set return-to-play criteria or test a return protocol; its activity guidance (24 to 48 hours of symptom-limited rest, then gradual activity) comes from the consensus guidelines it cites.
